```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",

  dpi = 100

This guide uses the bundled Cornwall GP data, described in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html).

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

Floating catchment area (FCA) methods combine demand, facility supply and
travel weights into an accessibility index. They differ in how they weight
travel. This guide computes three of them on the same inputs and compares the
results: the enhanced two-step FCA (E2SFCA) from [Getting started](spax.html),
the original 2SFCA and the modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA). For a fitted allocation
model with an outside option, see [Choosing an FCA index or an allocation
model](model-choice.html).

## The inputs

The inputs are those of [Getting started](spax.html): the WorldPop 2020
population grid (estimated residents per cell of about 1 km, a count rather
than a density), GP FTE excluding GPs in training, and travel minutes to each
mainland practice. The grid and the workforce come from different sources and
dates (2020 and 2026).

```{r inputs}
# Residents per grid cell, and travel minutes with one layer per practice
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")

# Mainland only: the Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]

# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice, then drop the
# empty margin the islands leave behind
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- crop(travel, pop)

# Layers must line up with the practice table and the population grid
stopifnot(
  identical(names(travel), gp$practice),
  compareGeom(pop, travel)
)

c(
  cells = sum(!is.na(values(pop))),
  practices = nrow(gp),
  residents = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  gp_fte = round(sum(gp$gp_fte_extg), 1)
)
```

[Preparing your own data](data-prep.html) explains these steps in detail.

## Three ways to weight travel

Each method gathers demand to practices with one set of weights, divides each
practice's supply by the demand it gathered, and spreads those ratios back to
cells with a second set of weights.

| Method | Weights when gathering demand | Weights when spreading ratios |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 2SFCA | 1 within 15 minutes, 0 beyond | The same |
| E2SFCA | Gaussian decay, scale 10 minutes | The same |
| M2SFCA | Gaussian decay, scale 10 minutes | The Gaussian weight squared |

The 15-minute threshold and the 10-minute scale are choices for this guide,
not estimates. With the Gaussian scale of 10 minutes, a practice 10 minutes
away keeps about 61% of its weight and one 20 minutes away about 14%.
`demand_normalize = "identity"` uses the weights unchanged when practices
gather demand, as in the original E2SFCA.

```{r methods}
twosfca <- spax_2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  threshold = 15,  # minutes
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

e2sfca <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity",
  id_col = "practice",  # matches supply rows to travel layers
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

m2sfca <- spax_m2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity",
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
```

Each result is a `spax` object whose `accessibility` member is a raster of GP
FTE per resident. The maps show all three in GP FTE per 1,000 residents on one
colour scale.

```{r methods-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one colour scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: E2SFCA changes smoothly, 2SFCA has sharp steps at the 15-minute catchment edges, and M2SFCA is lower throughout."}
# Stack the three surfaces and draw them on one shared colour scale
all_three <- 1000 * c(
  e2sfca$accessibility,
  twosfca$accessibility,
  m2sfca$accessibility
)
names(all_three) <- c(
  "E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "2SFCA, 15 min",
  "M2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min"
)
plot(
  all_three,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(values(all_three), na.rm = TRUE),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000")
)
```

## Compare the values

```{r compare}
# Cell values as plain vectors, per 1,000 residents, and residents per cell
per_1000 <- function(x) 1000 * values(x$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
a <- per_1000(e2sfca)
b <- per_1000(twosfca)
m <- per_1000(m2sfca)
p <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)

# Cell quantiles and the index of the average resident
describe <- function(x) {
  c(
    quantile(x, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
    resident_weighted = weighted.mean(x, p, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
round(
  rbind(
    E2SFCA = describe(a),
    `2SFCA` = describe(b),
    M2SFCA = describe(m)
  ),
  2
)

# Total supply per 1,000 residents, for comparison
round(1000 * sum(gp$gp_fte_extg) / sum(p, na.rm = TRUE), 2)

# An index of zero in 2SFCA means no practice within 15 minutes
c(
  residents_beyond_15_min = round(sum(p[b == 0], na.rm = TRUE)),
  correlation_2sfca = round(cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"), 2),
  correlation_m2sfca = round(cor(a, m, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
)
```

```{r compare-values, include = FALSE}
cor_2sfca <- round(cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_m2sfca <- round(cor(a, m, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
beyond_15 <- format(round(sum(p[b == 0], na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ",")
```

The quantiles describe grid cells, and most cells are rural. Weighting by
residents answers a different question: the index the average resident sees.
For E2SFCA and 2SFCA that average equals total GP FTE per 1,000 residents,
because each uses the same weights in both steps and every practice gathers
some demand. These indices redistribute the supply; they do not create or lose
any. M2SFCA does not keep that total: its squared weights are smaller than the
weights used to gather demand, so part of the supply is not spread back to
anyone, and it discounts most strongly the cells whose practices are far away.

The three surfaces broadly agree on where access is higher: E2SFCA correlates
at `r cor_2sfca` with 2SFCA and at `r cor_m2sfca` with M2SFCA across cells.
2SFCA shows sharp steps at the 15-minute edges and a longer upper tail, and
the `r beyond_15` residents with no practice within 15 minutes get an index of
zero. The decay versions change gradually instead. All three depend on choices, the threshold
or the decay scale, that this guide does not estimate from data. [The E2SFCA
calculation step by step](e2sfca-steps.html) rebuilds the E2SFCA and M2SFCA
surfaces from their parts.

The index has supply-per-demand units. It is not a share of people who use a
practice, a waiting time or an observed rate of care.
